rot.edge.ideia.ex1.e1: Now there are more pawns on the board. You play Black, and the board flips.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.e2: Look at the pawns: none can advance, because each has another pawn in front of it. They are blocked.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.e3: With the pawns stuck, only the kings move: whoever must move without a good king move is in zugzwang.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.e4: The white king's target is the pawn on c5. If your king moves away from it, the white king captures it.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.e5: To defend it, after each White move your king goes to the same rank as the white king and leaves an odd number of squares between them.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.e6: The pawn between the kings also counts as a square.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.livre.fala: Keep playing as Black and see how White attacks.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.livre.volta: Let's go back to the starting position. Suggest another move or click {verResposta}
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.p: Black to move. Think and suggest a move, or click {verResposta}
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.certo: Exactly! On a7, your king stands on the same rank as the white king, with three squares between them.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.revela: The best is to take the king to a7, on the same rank as the white king, with three squares between them.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.err.b6a6.1: After this move, White can win.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.err.b6a6.2: The white king goes to e6, on the same rank. There are three squares between the kings, counting the pawn on c6, and Black is to move: White has the opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.err.b6c7.1: After this move, White can win.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.err.b6c7.2: The white king goes to e6. If the black king returns to b6, the white king reaches d6 and keeps the opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.err.b6a5.1: After this move, White can win.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.err.b6a5.2: The white king goes to d7. If the black king returns to b6, the white king reaches d6 and keeps the opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.err.b6b7.1: After this move, White can win.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.err.b6b7.2: The white king goes to d7, on the same rank. Only c7 lies between the kings and Black is to move: White has the opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.l.1: Three squares between the kings, and White is to move: an odd number, so you have the opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.l.2: The white king approaches along the seventh rank, towards the black pawns.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.l.3: You answer on b7. Only c7 lies between the kings: you still have the opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.l.4: The white king steps down to d6 and attacks the pawn on c5.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.l.5: You defend with the king on b6. The pawn on c6 stands between the kings, and it counts as a square: just one, an odd number.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.l.6: You have the opposition. The white king cannot capture either pawn, because your king defends both.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.l.7: The pawns are locked and only the white king can move: in zugzwang, he has to step back.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.l.8: And if your king goes to c7? Only d7 lies between the kings, which also looks like an odd opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.l.8b: The white king goes to e6. Now the odd square would be a6, and from c7 your king cannot reach it: White gets the opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.l.9: That is why a7 is the right square: if the white king changes rank, your king follows him and leaves an odd number of squares.
rot.edge.ideia.ex1.l.10: Now let's see the attack: how White gets the opposition when it seems to belong to Black.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.e1: Now you play White. This position comes from a study by Brandon2021 on Lichess.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.e2: The pawns are still blocked. Your king wants to reach the black pawns on c5 and c6 to capture them.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.e3: The kings are on the same rank, with three squares between them, and White is to move. Black has the opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.e4: If your king comes closer, the black king follows on the same rank and keeps the number odd.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.e5: But notice: the pawn on c4 watches b5, and the pawn on a3 watches b4. The black king cannot go to those squares.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.livre.fala: Keep playing as White and see how Black defends.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.livre.volta: Let's go back to the starting position. Suggest another move or click {verResposta}
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.p: White to move. Think and suggest a move, or click {verResposta}
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.certo: Exactly! With your king on f5, the black king cannot keep the opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.revela: The best is to move the king away to f5. It looks strange, but this way the opposition becomes yours.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.err.e5d6.1: After this move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.err.e5d6.2: The black king goes to b6. Only the pawn on c6 lies between the kings and White is to move: Black has the opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.err.e5f6.1: After this move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.err.e5f6.2: The black king goes to b6, on the same rank. There are three squares between the kings and White is to move: Black has the opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.err.e5e6.1: After this move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.err.e5e6.2: The black king goes to a6, on the same rank. There are three squares between the kings and White is to move: Black has the opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.err.e5e4.1: After this move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.err.e5e4.2: The black king climbs to a6. On the sixth and seventh ranks no square is watched by a pawn, and he always follows your king.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.err.e5f4.1: After this move, White no longer wins: Black can draw.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.err.e5f4.2: The black king climbs to b6. On the sixth and seventh ranks no square is watched by a pawn, and he always follows your king.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.1: Now there are four squares between the kings, and Black is to move. To keep the opposition, the black king must leave an odd number.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.2: For that, he would have to go to b5, on the same rank. But the pawn on c4 watches that square.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.3: So the black king has to leave the fifth rank, and your king follows him on the new rank.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.4: The black king climbs to b6, to stay close to his pawns.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.5: You climb with him, to f6. Three squares between the kings: you have the opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.6: With no pawn move available, the black king has to move. He climbs to b7, hoping for a rank where you cannot follow him.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.7: You climb again, to f7. Three squares between the kings: it is the distant opposition, and it is still yours.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.13: Let's go back to the starting position. The key was the first move: the king on f5 left an even number of squares.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.14: The black king could not get back to an odd number, because the square he needed was watched by a pawn.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.15: Here g7 would also win, but e7 is safer: between two squares that leave an odd number, keep the one closer to the black pawns.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.curiosidades: This position appears in the chapter "Practical Endgame using opposition", from a study on the distant opposition published on Lichess by Brandon2021. The link opens the study.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.7b: The black king goes to a7. Four squares are left between the kings, an even number, and now White is to move.
rot.edge.demos.longe.1: Attack demonstration. Between the kings are b5, c5, d5, e5 and f5, the pawn included: five squares, and White is to move. Black has the opposition.
rot.edge.demos.longe.2: The white king steps back to f5. There are b5, c5, d5 and e5: four squares, an even number, and Black is to move.
rot.edge.demos.longe.3: To return to an odd number, the black king would need b5, but the c4 pawn watches that square.
rot.edge.demos.longe.4: So the black king must leave the fifth rank and climbs to a6.
rot.edge.demos.longe.5: The white king follows, to e6. There are b6, c6 and d6, the pawn included: three squares, an odd number, and Black is to move.
rot.edge.demos.longe.6: The decisive move was the first: the even number worked only because the c4 pawn watches b5. Afterwards, the white king follows the black king.
rot.edge.demos.escolha.1: Attack demonstration. Two squares leave an odd number between the kings: e6, with only d6 in between, and g6, with d6, e6 and f6. Which is right?
rot.edge.demos.escolha.2: With the king on e6, only d6 is left: an odd number. But the white king moves away from the black pawns.
rot.edge.demos.escolha.3: The black king counterattacks and runs to c4, toward the a3 pawn; the white king follows it along the fifth rank.
rot.edge.demos.escolha.4: The white king goes to e4 and to d3, but arrives too late: the black king is already on b3, next to the a3 pawn.
rot.edge.demos.escolha.5: The black king captures the a3 pawn and the game ends in a draw.
rot.edge.demos.escolha.6: Let us go back to the starting position and choose the other square, the one closer to the black pawns.
rot.edge.demos.escolha.7: With the king on g6, three squares remain, d6, e6 and f6: also odd. And the white king attacks the h5 pawn.
rot.edge.demos.escolha.8: The black king tries to run to the white pawns, via d7 and e7, but the white king captures the h5 pawn before it arrives.
rot.edge.demos.escolha.9: The white king returns to g6, and the h4 pawn runs free: White wins.
rot.edge.demos.oitava.1: Attack demonstration. The black king is trapped on the eighth rank: the e6 pawn guards d7 and f7, and e7 belongs to its own pawn. It can only move sideways.
rot.edge.demos.oitava.2: The white king wants to enter the seventh rank and reach d7, from where it captures the e7 pawn. To do that, it takes the opposition.
rot.edge.demos.oitava.3: The white king goes to b6, on the black king's diagonal: only c7 lies between them, and Black is to move. White has the opposition.
rot.edge.demos.oitava.4: On c6 it would be the black king that kept the opposition, answering on c8, face to face, and White would not get in.
rot.edge.demos.oitava.5: The black king goes to c8, facing the white king: the eighth is its only rank.
rot.edge.demos.oitava.6: The white king takes the direct opposition on c6, and the black king, forced to move, has to step aside.
rot.edge.demos.oitava.7: The black king goes to d8, to guard c7, but the white king enters the seventh rank via b7.
rot.edge.demos.oitava.8: The black king only has e8: c7 and c8 are next to the white king. And the white king goes on to c7, taking d8 from the black king.
rot.edge.demos.oitava.9: The black king only has f8: d8 is next to the white king, and d7 and f7 are guarded by the e6 pawn.
rot.edge.demos.oitava.10: The white king reaches d7 and attacks the e7 pawn. The black king cannot defend it: e8 is next to the white king, and f7 is guarded.
rot.edge.demos.oitava.11: The black king steps away, and the white king captures the e7 pawn. With the king in front of the e6 pawn, White wins.
rot.edge.demos.oitava.12: Keep the idea: a king trapped on the eighth rank is a king whose exits are guarded by a pawn. It only moves sideways, and the enemy king comes in along the seventh.
rot.edge.demos.contagem.1: Defence demonstration: now thinking from Black's side. The kings are on the sixth rank, and Black is to move.
rot.edge.demos.contagem.2: Between the kings are c6, with the pawn, and d6: two squares, an even number. Your king must leave an odd number.
rot.edge.demos.contagem.3: Your king goes to a6. Now b6, c6 and d6 are between them: three squares, and White is to move. The opposition is yours.
rot.edge.demos.contagem.4: The white king goes to d6 and threatens the pawn on c5.
rot.edge.demos.contagem.5: Your king returns to b6 and defends both pawns. Only c6 is between the kings, and White is to move: the opposition is still yours, and the white king must retreat.
rot.edge.demos.contagem.ponte: Your turn to play against the machine. First, an attack, with White.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.7c: Your king goes to e7: b7, c7 and d7 are left, three squares, and the opposition is still yours. On g7, the number would be odd too.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.7d: The black king goes back to b7 to defend the c6 pawn. c7 and d7 are left: two squares, an even number.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.7e: Your king goes to d7. Only c7 is left between the kings: an odd number, and the opposition is still yours.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.7f: The black king has to move and goes to a7. On b6, your king would go to d6 and keep the opposition.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.7g: Your king captures the c6 pawn, which was left undefended.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.7h: The black king goes to a6, but cannot reach the c5 pawn: the c4 pawn guards b5.
rot.edge.ideia.ex2.l.7i: Your king also captures the c5 pawn, and White wins: this is what the opposition was preparing.
rot.edge.demos.contagem.ponte2: Then a defence, with Black. Before each move, count the squares between the kings, pawns included.
rot.edge.pratica.ataque.enunciado: Play White: capture the d7 pawn.
rot.edge.pratica.ataque.fim: The d7 pawn is captured. The detour via g6 gave Black the move with the kings face to face on the f-file, and the black king stayed trapped on the eighth rank.
rot.edge.pratica.ataque.err.cedo.1: On f6, your king arrives too early: the black king goes to the f-file, in front of it, and the win slips away.
rot.edge.pratica.ataque.err.cedo.2: The black king goes to f8, on the same file. Only f7 is left between the kings, and White is to move: the opposition is Black's.
rot.edge.pratica.ataque.err.porta.1: This move leaves f7 free, the only square through which the black king leaves the eighth rank, and the win slips away.
rot.edge.pratica.ataque.err.porta.2: The black king leaves the eighth rank via f7, the only exit: off that rank, it is no longer trapped.
rot.edge.pratica.ataque.err.desce.1: This move takes your king away from the black king, and the win slips away.
rot.edge.pratica.ataque.err.desce.2: With your king far away, the black king has time: it keeps the opposition or leaves the eighth rank via f7, and White no longer wins.
rot.edge.pratica.ataque.err.solta.1: This move lets the black king leave the eighth rank: now it is Black who wins.
rot.edge.pratica.ataque.err.solta.2: The black king leaves the eighth rank and heads for the d6 pawn: your king, too far away, cannot defend it in time.
rot.edge.pratica.defesa.enunciado: Play Black and hold the draw.
rot.edge.pratica.defesa.fim: Your king followed the white king on every move and left no way through for the c4 pawn: the game ended in a draw.
rot.edge.pratica.defesa.err.longe.1: This move takes your king away from the white king, and he can no longer follow it: the draw slips away.
rot.edge.pratica.defesa.err.longe.2: The white king heads for the c5 pawn and captures it: your king, far away, cannot stop the c4 pawn in time.
rot.edge.pratica.defesa.err.f8.1: On f8, your king is one square farther from the white king than on e8 and cannot follow it: the draw slips away.
rot.edge.pratica.defesa.err.f8.2: The white king attacks the c5 pawn and captures it. Your king, one square behind, is too late to stop the c4 pawn.
rot.edge.pratica.defesa.err.b6.1: Your king must watch both b6 and c6: with this move, at least one of them is left free, and the draw slips away.
rot.edge.pratica.defesa.err.b6.2: The white king walks in through the free square and clears the way for the c4 pawn, which goes on to promote.
